<div class="fb-box">
<span class="fb-box-title">This page in one panel</span>
<dl>
<dt>The problem</dt>
<dd>Varieties do not rank the same everywhere. Separating a variety's
general merit from its response to environment is the central question
of a breeding programme.</dd>
<dt>In ASReml</dt>
<dd><code>asreml(yield ~ env, random = ~ gen + diag(env):gen)</code></dd>
<dt>In flexyBayes</dt>
<dd>The same, with <code>backend = "brms"</code>: the structured
genotype-by-environment terms are a brms capability.</dd>
<dt>What the posterior adds</dt>
<dd>Heritability, a ratio of variance components, is computed on the
draws, not through the delta method.</dd>
<dt>What it costs</dt>
<dd>The factor-analytic model, the workhorse of large METs, is refused
by both engines. Section 5 says what that means in practice.</dd>
</dl>
</div>

# 1. The MET question

`agridat::yan.winterwheat` is 18 winter wheat genotypes across 9 Ontario
environments, one yield per combination.


``` r
library(flexyBayes)
yw <- agridat::yan.winterwheat
table(nlevels(yw$gen), nlevels(yw$env))
#>     
#>      9
#>   18 1
```

Three models answer three different questions, and they nest.

**Main effect only.** `random = ~ gen` says varieties differ but rank
the same everywhere. One variance component.

**Plus interaction.** `random = ~ gen + gen:env` says varieties also
respond differently to environment, and measures that with a second
component. The ratio of the two is the question a breeder asks: how much
of the varietal signal survives across sites.

**Heterogeneous by environment.** `random = ~ diag(env):gen` says the
genotype spread itself differs between environments: a high-yielding
site may separate varieties more than a stressed one.

# 2. Main effect plus interaction


``` r
fit <- flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ gen + gen:env, data = yw,
                  backend = "brms", chains = 2L, n_samples = 1500L,
                  warmup = 750L, seed = 1L, verbose = FALSE,
                  mcmc_verbose = FALSE)
#> Warning: 172 of 3000 (6.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: 1 of 2 chains had an E-BFMI less than 0.3.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: Parts of the model have not converged (some Rhats are > 1.05). Be
#> careful when analysing the results! We recommend running more iterations and/or
#> setting stronger priors.
#> Warning: There were 172 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing
#> adapt_delta above 0.8 may help. See
#> http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
#> Warning: flexyBayes: the sampler may not have converged -- 13 parameters with
#> Rhat >= 1.10 (max 1.18); min effective sample size 10. Treat the posterior with
#> caution: increase `warmup` / `n_samples`, raise `control = list(adapt_delta =
#> 0.95)` where the run reported divergent transitions, simplify the model, or
#> supply a more informative prior. Inspect the full diagnostics with summary().
#> Silence this warning via options(flexyBayes.silence_convergence_warning =
#> TRUE).
tidy(fit, effects = "random")
#>         term  estimate  std.error   conf.low conf.high
#> 1     sd_gen 0.3972664 0.07974705 0.26415517 0.5667642
#> 2 sd_gen:env 0.1936228 0.10369591 0.01294438 0.3735759
#> 3      sigma 0.3124896 0.07870316 0.10435733 0.4152264
```

`sd_gen` is the spread of general merit, `sd_gen:env` the spread of
environment-specific deviation. When the second is comparable to the
first, selecting on an overall mean discards real information.

Heritability on an entry-mean basis follows from the components:


``` r
vc <- tidy(fit, effects = "random")
g  <- function(nm) vc$estimate[vc$term == nm]
n_env <- nlevels(yw$env)
g("sd_gen")^2 /
  (g("sd_gen")^2 + g("sd_gen:env")^2 / n_env + g("sigma")^2 / n_env)
#> [1] 0.9131229
```

Under REML this ratio needs the delta method for an interval. Under a
posterior the same computation done draw by draw gives one directly.

# 3. Heterogeneous genotype variance

`diag(env):gen` gives each environment its own genotype variance and no
correlation between them.


``` r
fit_d <- flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ diag(env):gen, data = yw,
                    backend = "brms", chains = 2L, n_samples = 1500L,
                    warmup = 750L, seed = 1L, verbose = FALSE,
                    mcmc_verbose = FALSE)
#> Warning: 2 of 2 chains had an E-BFMI less than 0.3.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
#> Warning: flexyBayes: the sampler may not have converged -- min effective sample
#> size 58. Treat the posterior with caution: increase `warmup` / `n_samples`,
#> raise `control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)` where the run reported divergent
#> transitions, simplify the model, or supply a more informative prior. Inspect
#> the full diagnostics with summary(). Silence this warning via
#> options(flexyBayes.silence_convergence_warning = TRUE).
head(tidy(fit_d, effects = "random"), 5)
#>              term  estimate std.error   conf.low conf.high
#> 1 sd_gen__envBH93 0.5445107 0.1747324 0.22629239 0.9448107
#> 2 sd_gen__envEA93 0.2902138 0.1590336 0.02022600 0.6149689
#> 3 sd_gen__envHW93 0.4243719 0.1619838 0.10329518 0.7480196
#> 4 sd_gen__envID93 0.2545703 0.1535943 0.01619144 0.5850794
#> 5 sd_gen__envKE93 0.6623831 0.1763153 0.36013842 1.0526940
```

One standard deviation per environment. Environments with a larger value
discriminate between varieties more strongly.

`us(env):gen` goes further and estimates the correlations between
environments as well, which is what tells you whether two sites are
effectively repeats of each other. It costs a parameter for every pair.

# 4. Known relationship matrices

Genomic selection replaces "genotypes are independent draws" with
"genotypes are related, and the relationship matrix says how".
`vm(gen, K)` supplies that matrix; `ped(animal, A)` is the same term
spelled for a pedigree.


``` r
set.seed(4)
n_g  <- 40
M    <- matrix(rbinom(n_g * 200, 2, 0.3), nrow = n_g)
Ks   <- scale(M)
K    <- tcrossprod(Ks) / ncol(Ks)
diag(K) <- diag(K) + 1e-6
dimnames(K) <- list(paste0("g", 1:n_g), paste0("g", 1:n_g))

dg <- data.frame(gen = factor(rep(paste0("g", 1:n_g), each = 3),
                              levels = paste0("g", 1:n_g)),
                 env = factor(rep(1:3, times = n_g)))
u  <- as.numeric(crossprod(chol(K), rnorm(n_g)))
dg$yield <- 5 + u[as.integer(dg$gen)] + rnorm(nrow(dg), 0, 0.4)

# INLA is given the precision, its documented carrier for this term
Q <- solve(K)
fit_g <- flexybayes(yield ~ env,
                    random = ~ vm(gen, cov = fb_cov(Q, type = "precision")),
                    data = dg, known_matrices = list(Q = Q),
                    backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE)
tidy(fit_g, effects = "random")
#>        term  estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high
#> 1     sigma 0.4234623 0.03439007 0.3610967 0.4958879
#> 2 sd_gen_id 0.9634469 0.12168608 0.7507251 1.2273908
```

The two engines take the relationship in different forms, and naming the
wrong one refuses instead of converting silently. INLA works from the
**precision**, the inverse of the relationship matrix, because its
latent field is parameterised that way and a sparse precision is what
makes the fit affordable. brms takes the **covariance** directly:


``` r
flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ vm(gen, K), data = dg,
           known_matrices = list(K = K), backend = "brms")
```

`fb_cov()` names the carrier: `covariance`, `precision`, `chol`,
`blocks` or `low_rank`. `backend = "auto"` picks an engine that accepts
the carrier you supplied.

The random effect is now correlated across genotypes according to `K`,
so a genotype with no phenotype of its own still receives a prediction
through its relatives. That is genomic prediction.

# 5. What is refused, and what to do instead

  </tr>

  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> <code>~ vm(g, K)</code>, <code>~ ped(a, A)</code> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> fits </td>
  </tr>

The factor-analytic model is the significant gap. `fa(env, k):gen`
approximates the environment covariance by a rank-`k` loading matrix
plus a diagonal, and it is the standard tool for a MET with many sites,
because `us()` becomes unaffordable. Neither engine emits it.

Where a MET is small enough, `us(env):gen` gives the full covariance and
`diag(env):gen` the heterogeneous-variance approximation. Where it is
not, ASReml remains the tool for the factor-analytic fit, and a
flexyBayes fit of a reduced model can be compared against it.

# 6. Pitfalls

**The relationship matrix must match the factor levels.** Row and column
order of `K` has to correspond to `levels(gen)`. A mismatch is a silent
reordering of the genotypes.

**Positive definiteness.** A genomic relationship matrix built from
markers is often singular. Adding a small ridge to the diagonal, as
above, is the usual remedy and the validator will refuse without it.

**Interaction terms are brms-only.** `gen:env` refuses on INLA, which
collapses the finest stratum. `auto` routes it.

**Heritability needs its basis stated.** Entry-mean and plot basis
differ by the divisors in the denominator. Report which one.
